common_name: Blue Umbrellas Hosta (Giant Rounded Blue-Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Blue Umbrellas is a Paul Aden introduction bred for enormous, deeply cupped, rounded blue-green leaves.

directions: Plant in spring or early fall in moist, organically enriched, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade, allowing plenty of room since Blue Umbrellas forms an imposing clump of huge, rounded, heavily cupped blue-green leaves that hold their frosty blue cast especially well when grown in fuller shade. The dramatic scale and bold, simple leaf shape make it an outstanding architectural anchor for a large woodland bed or shaded foundation planting, especially paired with finer-textured ferns or grasses for contrast. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes above the foliage in mid to late summer. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, since large-leaved hostas lose moisture faster than smaller cultivars, and divide only when the clump outgrows its space, as division sets a mature specimen back for several years.

common_name: Elvis Lives Hosta (Twisted Narrow-Leaf Hosta with Creamy Margin)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; a variegated sport of the novelty cultivar Praying Hands, sharing its unusual upright, twisted leaf habit.

directions: Elvis Lives is a variegated sport of the novelty hosta Praying Hands, carrying the same unusual narrow, twisted, upright-held leaves folded lengthwise like clasped hands, but edged in a creamy margin that adds extra interest to the already distinctive foliage shape. The narrow, vase-like growth habit sets it apart from typical broad-leaved hostas and makes it a good conversation-piece specimen in a container or at the front of a shaded bed. Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since too much direct sun fades the variegation and can scorch the thinner leaf substance. Pale lavender flowers appear in summer above the foliage. Divide only when clumps become congested, since novelty-form hostas are often slower to establish a full look than standard cultivars.

common_name: American Halo Hosta (Large Blue-Green Hosta with Wide Creamy-White Margin)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; American Halo is a large variegated sport valued for its broad, bright margin that lights up shaded corners.

directions: American Halo bears large, heavily corrugated blue-green leaves edged in a wide, irregular band of creamy white that brightens considerably as the season progresses, giving the plant strong visual weight in a shaded border without sacrificing the frosty blue tones typical of large hostas in this breeding line. Its substantial size and bold variegation make it an effective focal point when paired with smaller, fine-textured shade plants like ferns, heuchera, or astilbe. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on tall scapes in mid to late summer. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil in partial to full shade, since the white margin can scorch in strong afternoon sun, and water deeply during dry spells to keep the large leaves from stressing.

common_name: Maui Buttercups Hosta (Cupped Thick-Leaved Gold Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Maui Buttercups is grown for its thick, deeply cupped, glossy gold leaves that hold their bright color well through the season.

directions: Maui Buttercups forms a tidy, rounded mound of thick, deeply cupped, glossy golden-yellow leaves, the heavy substance and cupping making the foliage resistant to slug damage compared with thinner-leaved hosta cultivars. It brightens considerably with a few hours of morning sun, which deepens the gold color without the scorching that stronger afternoon sun would cause. Its compact, well-behaved size fits neatly into a shaded rock garden, container planting, or the front of a mixed woodland border. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil and divide only when the clump becomes crowded, since compact gold hostas are slower to need division than larger, faster-spreading cultivars.

common_name: T Rex Hosta (Giant Dark Green Corrugated Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; T Rex is one of the largest hosta cultivars available, needing several years and a great deal of room to reach full size.

directions: T Rex bears enormous, heavily corrugated, dark green leaves on a mounding plant that ranks among the largest hosta cultivars grown, rivaling giants like Empress Wu and Sum and Substance for sheer scale in a shaded landscape. Give it several years to reach mature size and allow at least five to six feet of space, since crowding a giant hosta shortens its display and makes routine care harder. Its massive, bold-textured leaves make an outstanding focal specimen at the back of a woodland border or as a stand-alone specimen near a shaded patio. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in summer, though the foliage itself is the main attraction. Plant in moist, organically enriched soil in partial shade, water deeply and regularly, especially while establishing, and avoid moving or dividing it once it reaches full size.

common_name: Coast to Coast Hosta (Giant Wavy-Margined Chartreuse-Gold Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; a Hans Hansen introduction bred for enormous, glowing gold leaves with a distinctive wavy margin.

directions: Coast to Coast produces very large, smooth, glowing chartreuse-to-gold leaves with a gently undulating, wavy margin, the bright color intensifying through the season as the leaves mature and holding up well with a few hours of morning sun. Its imposing size and luminous color make it an outstanding focal point for lighting up a shaded corner that would otherwise read as dark and flat. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes above the foliage in summer. Give it plenty of room to spread, since crowding shortens the display of a giant gold hosta, and plant in moist, organically enriched soil in partial shade, watering deeply during dry spells to keep the large leaves from stressing.

common_name: White Feather Hosta (Novelty Hosta with White Spring Foliage Turning Green)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; a novelty hosta grown for its unusual color-changing foliage rather than for vigor, since the near-white spring leaves lack chlorophyll and are slow to establish.

directions: White Feather is a striking novelty hosta whose new spring leaves emerge nearly pure white, gradually developing streaks of green through early summer until the mature foliage turns mostly green by the time flowers appear, a color transformation caused by the leaves lacking chlorophyll when they first unfurl. Because the white spring growth cannot photosynthesize efficiently, the plant is slower and less vigorous than typical green or gold hostas and benefits from being sited where its dramatic early-season color can be enjoyed up close, such as a shaded rock garden or container. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer once the foliage has greened up. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil in partial to full shade, and avoid dividing frequently, since this novelty cultivar needs time to build strength between divisions.

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; a true miniature hosta suited to rock gardens, troughs, and the front edge of a shaded bed.

directions: Cracker Crumbs forms a tiny, tidy mound of small, thick, gold-to-chartreuse leaves only an inch or two long, brightening to a clearer gold with a bit of morning sun and staying more chartreuse in fuller shade. Its diminutive scale makes it a good choice for edging a shaded path, tucking into a rock garden pocket, or growing in a shallow container where a full-sized hosta would be out of proportion. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer, proportionally sized to match the tiny foliage. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil, and keep a close eye out for slug damage, since a single slug can do serious damage to a miniature hosta's small total leaf area. Divide only occasionally, as miniature hostas increase slowly compared with larger cultivars.

common_name: Little Aurora Hosta (Small Rounded Gold Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; a long-popular small gold hosta valued for its neat, rounded habit and reliable color.

directions: Little Aurora forms a neat, small mound of rounded, slightly cupped golden-yellow leaves that hold their bright color well through the season, especially with a few hours of morning sun to bring out the fullest gold tone. Its compact, well-behaved size and dependable performance have kept it a mainstay small hosta for edging shaded borders, filling rock garden pockets, and mass planting under trees where a uniform low groundcover is wanted. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes held just above the foliage in summer. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil in partial shade, water during dry spells, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the color bright and the habit tidy.

common_name: Sun Mouse Hosta (Miniature Thick-Leaved Gold Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; a gold-leaved sport in the popular 'Mouse Ears' line of thick-substanced miniature hostas.

directions: Sun Mouse belongs to the popular Mouse Ears line of miniature hostas prized for unusually thick, heavy-substanced leaves that resist slug damage far better than thinner-leaved miniatures, here in a bright gold color that deepens with a bit of morning sun. Its tiny, rounded leaves and slow, dense growth habit suit a shaded rock garden, trough planting, or the front edge of a mixed border where a full-sized hosta would overwhelm the space. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer above the compact mound. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil in partial shade, and expect slow but steady growth, since Mouse Ears-type hostas build size gradually and rarely need frequent division.

common_name: Frosted Mouse Ears Hosta (Miniature Blue-Green Hosta with White Margin)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; a variegated sport of the popular thick-leaved miniature Blue Mouse Ears.

directions: Frosted Mouse Ears is a variegated sport of Blue Mouse Ears, keeping the same tiny, thick, rounded blue-green leaves but edged in a crisp white margin that gives the whole plant a frosted look. Like its parent, the exceptionally thick leaf substance resists slug damage better than most miniature hostas, making it a durable choice for a shaded rock garden or container where slug pressure is a concern. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer above the dense, slow-growing mound. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil in partial to full shade, since strong sun can scorch the white-margined leaves, and expect slow, steady growth typical of Mouse Ears-type miniature hostas.

common_name: Pineapple Upside Down Cake Hosta (Rippled Gold-Centered Dark-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; a whimsically named modern hosta grown for its rippled gold center framed by a dark green margin.

directions: Pineapple Upside Down Cake bears rounded, heavily rippled leaves with a bright gold center framed by a contrasting dark green margin, a reversed variegation pattern that makes the gold coloring the dominant feature rather than a thin accent edge. The pronounced rippling and strong color contrast give it good garden presence in a mid-sized clump, working well as a specimen among finer-textured ferns and shade perennials. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Grow in moist, organically enriched soil in partial shade, since a bit of morning sun helps deepen the gold color without scorching the leaf margins, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain a vigorous, well-colored display.
